title: API Gateway: Complete Architecture
description: Design a horizontally scalable API gateway that routes, authenticates, and observes traffic to hundreds of internal microservices.

data.text: Design a single ingress layer for 200+ internal microservices that terminate TLS, authenticate and authorize every request, route to the correct upstream version, enforce rate limits and quotas, and expose consistent metrics — while adding under 5 ms of latency at P99 and surviving the loss of an entire availability zone.

terms.definition: North-south is traffic entering the cluster from clients (handled by the gateway). East-west is service-to-service traffic inside the cluster (handled by a service mesh).
The mechanism by which the gateway learns healthy upstream addresses — either a control plane pushing endpoint lists, or DNS-based discovery.
A declarative mapping from request attributes (host, path, header, method) to an upstream cluster, with optional transforms and weighted splits.
Validating JWTs and API keys at the gateway so that downstream services can trust a signed identity header instead of re-validating every token.
Refusing or queuing work when an upstream is saturated, so a slow service cannot exhaust the gateway's connection pools and threads.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Dynamic Routing: map host plus path prefix to an upstream service, including weighted splits for canary releases
TLS Termination: manage certificates for hundreds of hostnames with automated rotation
Authentication: validate OAuth2 JWTs, API keys, and mTLS client certificates at the edge
Authorization: enforce coarse-grained scopes and route-level allowlists
Rate Limiting & Quotas: per API key, per user, and per route limits
Request/Response Transformation: header injection, path rewriting, and payload size limits
Observability: emit structured access logs, trace context propagation, and per-route RED metrics

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Low Latency Overhead: under 5 ms P99 added compared to a direct call
High Throughput: sustain 500,000 requests per second per region with horizontal scaling
High Availability: no single point of failure; survive the loss of a whole AZ with zero customer-visible errors
Instant Configuration: route changes propagate in under 5 seconds without a deploy or restart
Safe Failure: an unhealthy upstream must be ejected quickly and recovered automatically

data.text: Clients hit a global anycast DNS and CDN layer, which forwards to a regional load balancer. The gateway fleet is stateless and shares nothing except the control plane that pushes route and certificate configuration.

data.caption: API Gateway Architecture: Global DNS/CDN, Regional Load Balancer, Stateless Gateway Fleet, Control Plane for Routes, and Upstream Services

data.text: Every request passes through an ordered filter chain. Ordering matters: authenticate cheaply before doing expensive work, and reject early rather than deep in the stack.

items: TLS handshake and SNI-based certificate selection
Connection-level protections: IP allow/deny lists and DDoS shape
Request validation: size limit, header sanity, and allowed methods
Authentication: parse and verify the JWT or API key; reject with 401 if invalid
Authorization: check route-level scope requirements; reject with 403 if insufficient
Rate limit evaluation against the distributed counter; reject with 429 if exceeded
Route match: select the upstream cluster and apply any weighted split
Apply transforms: header injection, path rewrite, and request id generation
Forward to upstream with a bounded timeout and retry policy
Capture response: metrics, access log, and trace span

data.text: Each upstream cluster uses **outlier detection** plus **least-request** balancing. Passive health checks eject an endpoint after a configured number of consecutive 5xx responses; active health checks probe it in the background to bring it back.

data.title: Envoy-style gateway configuration
data.code:
static_resources:
  listeners:
    - name: https_in
      address: { socket_address: { address: 0.0.0.0, port_value: 443 } }
      filter_chains:
        - filters:
            - name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
              typed_config:
                "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.network.http_connection_manager.v3.HttpConnectionManager
                stat_prefix: ingress
                route_config:
                  name: local_routes
                  virtual_hosts:
                    - name: api
                      domains: [ "api.example.com" ]
                      routes:
                        - match: { prefix: "/orders" }
                          route:
                            cluster: orders_service
                            timeout: 3s
                            retry_policy:
                              retry_on: "5xx,reset,connect-failure"
                              num_retries: 2
                              per_try_timeout: 1s
                        - match: { prefix: "/" }
                          route: { cluster: default_service, timeout: 5s }
                http_filters:
                  - name: envoy.filters.http.jwt_authn
                  - name: envoy.filters.http.local_ratelimit
                  - name: envoy.filters.http.router

  clusters:
    - name: orders_service
      type: EDS                                  # endpoints from the control plane
      eds_cluster_config: { eds_config: { ads: {} } }
      lb_policy: LEAST_REQUEST
      circuit_breakers:
        thresholds:
          - priority: DEFAULT
            max_connections: 1024
            max_pending_requests: 1024
            max_retries: 3
      outlier_detection:
        consecutive_5xx: 5
        interval: 10s
        base_ejection_time: 30s
        max_ejection_percent: 50

faqs.question: Should the gateway do business logic or stay purely a router?
faqs.answer: Keep it a router plus cross-cutting concerns. Business logic in the gateway means every service team must coordinate a shared deploy to change behaviour, and the gateway becomes a single point of coordination. Anything that differs per service belongs in the service; anything identical across all services belongs at the gateway.

faqs.question: How do you push route changes in under 5 seconds without restarting?
faqs.answer: Run a control plane that implements the xDS protocol (or Consul/Nacos equivalent). Gateways hold a long-lived gRPC stream to the control plane and receive incremental updates. Configuration is validated and canaried before it reaches production, and each node applies changes atomically so a partially applied route table is never served.

faqs.question: Why not let every service validate its own JWT?
faqs.answer: You can, and many teams do for defense in depth. But validating at the edge lets you reject unauthenticated traffic before it consumes any downstream capacity, and it centralises JWKS caching. The usual compromise is edge validation for the happy path plus local validation for zero-trust at the service boundary.

faqs.question: How do you avoid the gateway becoming a single point of failure?
faqs.answer: The gateway fleet is stateless, so it scales horizontally and any node can serve any request. Deploy across at least three availability zones behind a regional load balancer. The only shared dependencies are the service registry and the rate-limit store, both of which must themselves be replicated and must fail open rather than block traffic.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The gateway owns cross-cutting concerns; services own business logic
A stateless fleet plus a pushed control plane gives instant config and horizontal scale
Authenticate and rate limit early so expensive work is never done for unwanted traffic
Outlier detection plus circuit breakers stop one sick service from consuming the whole edge
Fail open for availability, fail closed only for security-critical paths
data.takeaway: An API gateway is a stateless, control-plane-driven ingress tier that centralises routing, security, and observability while deliberately staying free of business logic.
